about: Confusion pairs (W17). kind: sense (two senses of one headword; a plain headword such as "temper" names its everyday sense, given in the entry's everyday field), lookalike (alike in form or sound, unlike in meaning) or nearmiss (close in meaning, and the SAT sets one against the other). words are library slugs, or plain words that are not library entries. tell is the one line that separates them. Entries' own lookalikes are derived by the build and are not repeated here.

entries.tell: As an adjective, abstract means existing only as an idea; as a noun, an abstract is the short summary printed before a research article.
An apparent flaw may be plain to see or may only seem real; if the passage hints the look misleads (her apparent calm hid panic), it is the seeming sense.
Land or stock that appreciates rises in value, with no object; to appreciate a problem is to grasp how serious it is.
Assets appreciate by rising in price; people appreciate a favor by being grateful for it.
To appreciate the difficulty of a task is to understand it fully, not to be thankful for it.
Assume that something is true and you suppose it without proof; assume a role, a duty or a name and you take it on.
To compromise safety, health or one's principles is to weaken or endanger them; to compromise with a rival is to settle by each side giving ground.
Muscles, metals and economies contract by shrinking; people contract an illness by catching it.
A contract is a signed agreement, but a market or a metal that contracts simply becomes smaller.
To contract measles is to catch it; nothing is signed or agreed.
A curious person is eager to learn; a curious detail or habit is strange. Ask whether the word describes someone's interest or something's oddness.
Defer a decision and you put it off; defer to an expert and you give way to her judgment. The word to marks the yielding sense.
To elaborate on a point (verb) is to add detail; an elaborate plan (adjective) is intricate, with many parts.
People endure hardship by putting up with it; a tradition that endures simply lasts. With an object it is withstand; without one, last.
To grant a request or a license is to give it formally; to grant that a point is true is to admit it before arguing further.
Keen on or keen to means eager; a keen eye, ear or mind is sharp and quick to notice.
Maintain a road or a machine and you keep it in working order; maintain that a claim is true and you insist on it.
A modest person does not boast; a modest gain, budget or house is merely small.
The adjective objective means unbiased and based on facts; the noun an objective is a goal to reach.
The verb obscure means hide or cloud (fog obscured the peak); an obscure poet is little known.
A partial list is incomplete; a partial referee favors one side. Partial to someone also means fond of them.
Peculiar on its own usually means odd; peculiar to means belonging only to, as a plant peculiar to one island.
A prompt reply comes without delay (adjective); to prompt a reply is to cause it (verb).
To qualify a claim is to narrow it with a condition or exception; to qualify for a prize is to meet its requirements.
To render something useless is to make it so; to render a scene, a song or a role is to portray or perform it.
To resolve a dispute (verb) is to settle it; a person's resolve (noun) is firm determination.
To sanction a plan is to approve it officially; sanctions imposed on a country are penalties. The verb usually approves; the plural noun punishes.
To stem a flow is to stop it; to stem from a cause is to arise from it. The word from is the tell.
A field, an experiment or a search yields something by producing it; a person yields to pressure by giving way.
To temper criticism with praise is to soften it; a temper is a tendency to get angry.
To champion a cause is to fight for it; a champion is the winner of a contest.
To arrest a decline or a disease is to halt it; police arrest a suspect by taking him into custody.
A command of a language or a subject is mastery of it; a command is an order to be obeyed.
To check inflation or an advance is to hold it back; to check an answer is to make sure it is right.
A voice that betrays nervousness reveals it without meaning to; betraying a friend is being disloyal.
To entertain an idea or a doubt is to consider it; to entertain guests is to amuse them.
A grave error or threat is very serious; a grave is a burial place.
The verb intimate (IN-tuh-mate) means hint at; the adjective intimate (IN-tuh-mit) means close and personal.
As a verb, to occasion a change is to bring it about; as a noun, an occasion is an event or a time.
Pedestrian prose or ideas are dull and ordinary; a pedestrian is a person traveling on foot.
To reflect on a choice is to think carefully about it; a mirror reflects light.
Reservations about a plan are doubts; a reservation at a hotel is a booking.
A sound argument or method is well reasoned and reliable; a sound is a noise.
Spare prose or decor is plain and lean; a spare key or tire is extra.
To subject samples to heat is to make them undergo it; a subject is a topic or a person under study.
A plan found wanting is lacking or not good enough; wanting a thing is desiring it.
In the wake of an event means in its aftermath; to wake is to stop sleeping.
To advance a theory or an argument is to put it forward; troops advance by moving forward.
To air a grievance or a view is to express it publicly; to air a room is to let fresh air in.
To coin a word or phrase is to invent it; a coin is a piece of metal money.
A request couched in polite terms is phrased that way; a couch is a sofa.
To credit a discovery to someone is to attribute it to that person; to credit an account is to add money to it.
To execute a plan or a design is to carry it out; to execute a prisoner is to put him to death.
To exercise caution, power or a right is to use it; to exercise is to work out.
To fashion a tool out of bone is to shape or make it; fashion is the current style in clothing.
To field questions or complaints is to deal with them as they come; a field is open land.
Interest or energy that flags is weakening; to flag an error is to mark it for attention.
A plan or a ship that founders fails or sinks; a founder is a person who starts an organization.
The gravity of a situation is its seriousness; gravity is also the force that pulls objects toward the ground.
To harbor doubts or a grudge is to hold it privately in mind; a harbor is a port for ships.
To hold that a claim is true is to maintain it; to hold a cup is to grasp it.
Experience that informs an artist's work shapes it; to inform someone is to tell them facts.
A marked change or difference is clearly noticeable; a marked box has a mark written on it.
Minute (my-NOOT) means extremely small; a minute (MIN-it) is sixty seconds.
A moving speech stirs the emotions; a moving train is in motion.
To negotiate a steep trail or an obstacle is to get through it; to negotiate a deal is to bargain.
Critics who pan a film criticize it harshly; a camera that pans sweeps across a scene.
A pressing need or question is urgent; pressing a button is pushing down on it.
To realize a goal or an ambition is to achieve it; to realize a fact is to become aware of it.
To rehearse old arguments or grievances is to repeat or recount them; actors rehearse to practice.
To shoulder a cost or a duty is to take on the burden; to shoulder past someone is to push aside with the body.
In American usage, to table a proposal is to set it aside for later; a table is a piece of furniture.
To tender a resignation or a bid is to offer it formally; tender care is gentle.
To venture a guess or an opinion is to offer it cautiously; a venture is a risky undertaking.
To weather a storm or a crisis is to come through it; rock that has weathered has been worn away by exposure.
A scientific bent is a natural inclination toward science; a bent nail is curved.
A conviction is a firm belief; in court, a conviction is a verdict of guilty.
To discount a rumor or a warning is to treat it as unimportant; to discount a price is to lower it.
A fine distinction is subtle or precise; feeling fine means feeling okay.
A fluid situation is likely to change; a fluid is a liquid or a gas.
To husband resources is to use them sparingly; a husband is a married man.
To mount a campaign or an exhibit is to organize and begin it; to mount a horse is to climb onto it.
A stock phrase or character is standard and predictable; stock is shares in a company or goods kept on hand.
A task that taxes one's patience strains it; a tax is money owed to a government.
A novel's treatment of a theme is the way it handles that theme; medical treatment is care for an illness.
An account of an event is an explanation or a report of it; a bank account is a record of money held.
To conduct a study or a survey is to carry it out; to conduct an orchestra is to lead it.
A cool reception is unfriendly or unenthusiastic; in casual speech, cool means impressive.
A critical step or moment is crucial; a critical review finds fault.
A retiring person is shy and avoids attention; a retiring worker is ending a career.
A scientist's standing is her status or reputation; standing is also being on one's feet.
The verb appropriate (-ate) means take for one's own use, often without permission; the adjective appropriate (-it) means suitable.
An express promise or purpose is clearly stated; an express train makes few stops.
A patent falsehood is obvious; a patent is a legal right to an invention.
The moon waxes as it grows; to wax a floor is to polish it. Wax is the opposite of wane.
Critics who hail a book praise it publicly; to hail a taxi is to call out to it.
Lean years or harvests are meager; to lean on a wall is to rest against it.
Grounds for a complaint are the reasons for it; the ground is the surface of the earth.
In the SAT sense, plastic means easily shaped, as a young brain is plastic; everyday plastic is a synthetic material.
To dwell on a mistake is to keep thinking or talking about it; to dwell in a place is to live there.
A discriminating reader judges quality well; discriminating against people is treating them unfairly.
An arresting image is striking and holds attention; arresting a suspect is taking him into custody.
To act with dispatch is to act with speed and efficiency; to dispatch a messenger is to send him off.
Renege is going back on a promise or deal you made; forsake is abandoning a person, place or belief entirely.
Jettison is throwing out something no longer wanted, such as cargo or a plan; forsake is deserting what you were loyal to.
Rescind is officially canceling a law, rule or offer; renege is failing to keep your own promise.
Theoretical means based on theory rather than practice; hypothetical means supposed for the sake of argument.
Intangible stresses that a thing can't be touched or easily measured, such as goodwill; abstract stresses that it exists as an idea, not a concrete case.
To generalize is to draw a broad rule from particular cases; to extrapolate is to extend a known trend beyond the range actually measured.
Overarching names one idea or goal that ties all the parts together; comprehensive means covering nearly every part.
Adequate is just enough for the purpose; ample is more than enough.
A plethora is an excess, often more than is wanted; myriad simply means countless, with no complaint.
Prolific describes a producer, as an author who writes many books; abundant describes the supply itself.
Acknowledge is to recognize openly, often neutrally; concede is to admit, reluctantly, a point that favors the other side.
Assent is agreeing to a proposal or a statement; concede is admitting, often unwillingly, that the other side is right on a point.
To notice a warning is only to perceive it; to heed it is to pay attention and act on it.
Resigned means accepting what can't be changed without being pleased about it; content means actually satisfied.
Embrace is accepting eagerly; tolerate is putting up with something you may dislike.
Inadvertent means done by accident, without meaning to; spontaneous means done on impulse, meant but unplanned.
Impulsive carries a warning, acting without thinking; spontaneous is usually neutral or approving, unplanned and natural.
Serendipitous is a happy discovery made while looking for something else; fortuitous is anything that happens by chance, now usually lucky chance.
Glean is gathering bit by bit from scattered sources; derive is obtaining from one source, often by reasoning.
You attain a goal or a level by effort; you procure an object or a supply by getting hold of it.
Appropriate is taking for one's own use, often without the right to; procure is obtaining, usually properly.
Vivacious describes a lively, attractive personality; animated describes lively talk or motion at a given moment, as an animated debate.
Dynamic means changing in an energetic, often productive way; volatile means changing unpredictably and dangerously.
Intervene is stepping into a situation to change its course; intercede is stepping in on someone's behalf, to plead for them.
To approach a problem is just to begin taking it up; to grapple with it is to struggle hard with it.
To field questions is to answer them as they come; to deflect them is to turn them aside without answering.
Endorse is publicly approving something another has proposed; espouse is adopting a cause or belief as your own.
Tout is promoting eagerly, often with hype and doubtful claims; advocate is arguing in favor with reasons.
Lobby is pressing officials or lawmakers to act; advocate is arguing for something before any audience.
Propose is putting an idea forward for consideration; advocate is arguing that it should be adopted.
Adapt is changing to suit new conditions; alter is changing in some respect, for any reason.
Overhaul is rebuilding or reforming thoroughly; amend is making a specific change or correction, as to a law.
Amend is making a targeted correction or addition, especially to a law or a document; revise is reworking a whole text after review.
Apprehensive means uneasy about what might happen; distraught means already deeply upset by what has happened.
Trepidation is fearful expectation of what is coming; anticipation is expectation that can be eager.
Onerous is a burden to bear, such as duties or rules; arduous is a task that takes hard, tiring effort, such as a climb.
Daunting stresses that a task discourages the person facing it; formidable can praise, meaning impressively powerful, as a formidable opponent.
Grueling means exhausting to the point of punishment; strenuous means requiring great effort, not necessarily punishing.
Pompous is solemnly self-important in manner or speech; pretentious is trying to seem more cultured or important than one is.
Haughty is proud and aloof toward others; condescending is superior while seeming to stoop kindly toward them.
Pride can be healthy self-respect; hubris is overconfidence that invites a fall.
Allege is claiming without proof, often of wrongdoing; assert is stating firmly, with no hint that the claim is unproven.
Contend is arguing for your own position; concede is admitting a point in favor of the other side.
Proclaim is announcing publicly and formally, to many; assert is stating firmly, in public or not.
Evade is escaping something you ought to face, such as a question or a tax; circumvent is finding a way around a rule or an obstacle.
Abstain is choosing not to take part, especially in a vote or an indulgence; refrain is holding back from an action, as to refrain from comment.
Shun is avoiding a person or group, often to exclude them; eschew is deliberately avoiding a practice or a thing, as to eschew jargon.
Benign means harmless; beneficial means actively helpful.
Salutary is beneficial, often through an unpleasant lesson, as a salutary warning; wholesome is good for health or character in a pleasant way.
Allocate is distributing for a set purpose, as to allocate funds; bestow is giving as an honor.
Endow is providing lasting funds or a quality, as endowed with talent; bestow is presenting a gift or honor on an occasion.
Subjective means shaped by personal views and feelings; partial means unfairly favoring one side.
Tendentious describes writing slanted to push a view; partisan describes a person or group loyal to one side or party.
A bias is any systematic lean, even in data or instruments; a prejudice is an unfair judgment of people formed before knowing them.
Intrepid is fearless and admired; reckless is heedless of danger and blamed.
Audacious is boldly daring, often admired; brazen is shamelessly bold, and blamed for it.
Placid describes a calm temperament or still water, sometimes dull; tranquil describes a peaceful place or state.
Equanimity is calm under strain from someone who still cares; apathy is not caring at all.
Proficient means competent through practice; adept means highly skilled, a step above.
Adroit is skillful and quick in handling things or people; shrewd is sharp in judging what serves one's interest.
Evoke is calling up a memory, image or feeling; elicit is drawing out a response or an answer from someone.
Incite is stirring people up to act, usually violently or unlawfully; provoke is causing a reaction, often anger.
A catalyst triggers or speeds up a change without being the change itself; an impetus is the driving force or motive behind it.
Induce is bringing about or persuading; coerce is forcing by pressure or threats.
Wary is alert to a particular danger; timid is fearful by temperament, lacking courage.
Prudent stresses caution about risk; judicious stresses sound judgment in weighing a choice.
Vigilant is watchful for danger as it comes; circumspect is careful to consider consequences before acting or speaking.
Definitive means final and authoritative, as a definitive study; unequivocal means leaving no doubt about what is meant, as an unequivocal no.
Inevitable means certain to happen sometime; imminent means about to happen soon.
Incontrovertible describes evidence or facts that can't be disputed; unequivocal describes a statement that can't be misread.
Desultory is aimless and halfhearted, lacking purpose; haphazard is random, lacking a plan or an order.
Chaotic stresses total disorder; tumultuous stresses noise and turbulent upheaval.
Articulate is expressing an idea clearly in words; elaborate is adding more detail to an idea already stated.
Delineate is marking out the exact boundaries or features of something; describe is telling what it is like.
Explicate is interpreting a text in detail, line by line; elucidate is making any obscure point clear.
A rationale is the actual reasoning behind a choice; a rationalization is a self-serving excuse invented afterward.
Lucid means clear and easy to understand; coherent means logically connected, so the parts fit together.
Synthesize is combining ideas or sources into something new; integrate is fitting a part into an existing whole.
Coalesce is coming together of its own accord, as droplets or factions do; amalgamate is merging organizations or materials, often by design.
Attribute a result to any cause, good or bad; credit someone with it usually implies praise.
A complement completes or pairs well with something; a supplement adds to what is already complete.
Vie is competing eagerly for something, as to vie for a prize; rival as a verb is matching or equaling, as few cities rival Paris.
Intricate praises fine, complex detail; convoluted faults needless, tangled complexity.
Nuanced means alert to fine distinctions; sophisticated means highly developed, complex or worldly.
Conform is matching accepted norms or standards; comply is obeying a specific rule or request.
Docile describes a quiet, easily led temperament; compliant describes obeying rules or requests, sometimes too readily.
Extensive is large in range or amount; comprehensive is complete, covering nearly everything that matters.
Holistic means treating the whole as more than its parts, looking at how they interact; comprehensive means covering all the parts.
Surreptitious stresses a sneaky act done unnoticed; clandestine stresses an organized secret, as a clandestine meeting.
Furtive describes shifty, guilty-looking behavior, as a furtive glance; covert describes an operation that is officially secret.
Veil is partly hiding or disguising, as a veiled threat; conceal is hiding completely.
Concise is brief and complete, a compliment; terse is brief to the point of rudeness.
Laconic describes a person who uses few words by habit; terse describes a reply cut short, often curtly.
Pithy is brief and full of meaning or wit; succinct is simply brief and clear.
Summarize is restating only the main points, more briefly; paraphrase is restating all of it in other words.
Empirical means drawn from observation or experiment; theoretical means drawn from theory and reasoning.
Specific means particular rather than general; concrete means observable and real rather than abstract.
Tangible means real enough to touch or measure, as tangible results; palpable means so strong it can almost be felt, as palpable tension.
Concur is people agreeing; coincide is events happening at the same time, or things matching.
Consensus is general agreement of nearly everyone; a majority is merely more than half.
Compatible means able to exist together without conflict; consistent means in agreement across cases or with itself.
Blatant stresses that a wrong is done openly, without hiding it; flagrant stresses that it is shockingly serious.
Conspicuous means easy to notice; salient means most important or relevant, standing out as key.
Perpetuate means keep something going; perpetrate means commit a crime or a wrong.
Persevere is admired persistence toward a goal; persist can be neutral or unwelcome, as a cough persists.
Protract means drag out, usually tediously; prolong means make last longer, neutral or welcome.
Abridge is shortening a text while keeping its essentials; truncate is cutting off a part, often abruptly.
Curtail cuts something back or short; curb holds something in check.
Conventional means following usual practice; orthodox means following accepted doctrine, as in religion or a scientific theory.
Reciprocal means given in return, one to the other; mutual means shared by both at once.
Venal means open to bribery; mercenary means motivated chiefly by money.
Nefarious means wicked or criminal in intent; egregious means shockingly bad, as an egregious error, not necessarily wicked.
Concoct is making something up, often a false story; formulate is carefully developing a plan or an idea.
Originate is being the first to create or the place something begins; generate is producing, as a power plant generates electricity.
Plausible seems reasonable but may be unproven; credible is believable on the evidence.
Tenable means able to be defended against attack; valid means logically sound.
Disparage is belittling, calling something unimportant or poor; deride is mocking it with open contempt.
Criticize is pointing out faults; condemn is the strongest, declaring something wrong.
Dismissive treats something as not worth attention; disdainful looks down on it as beneath one.
Derisive means mocking; derisory means so small it is laughable, as a derisory offer.
Callous is unfeeling toward others' suffering; ruthless is pitiless in pursuing a goal.
Vindictive seeks revenge for a wrong; spiteful wants to hurt or annoy with no wrong required.
Malicious describes an act meant to harm; malevolent describes a wish or a nature bent on harm.
A pretext is a false reason given to hide the real one; a pretense is a false show, as a pretense of interest.
Evasive describes a person dodging a question on purpose; elusive describes something hard to find, catch or grasp.
Disingenuous is pretending to be more innocent or less informed than one is; hypocritical is claiming standards one does not follow.
Devious is sneaky and indirect in getting one's way; duplicitous is two-faced, saying one thing and doing another.
Falter is losing strength or momentum, perhaps briefly; flounder is struggling clumsily, as if stuck.
Stagnate is ceasing to grow or move; languish is weakening or suffering from neglect over time.
Wane is gradual weakening after a peak, as the moon or influence wanes; dwindle is shrinking in number or size, as savings dwindle.
Erode is wearing away gradually by friction or pressure; dissipate is scattering and vanishing, or wasting.
Infringe is violating a right or rule by encroaching on it, as on a patent; transgress is crossing a moral or legal limit.
Contravene is going against a rule or law, even unknowingly; flout is disregarding it openly and scornfully.
Belated describes something that comes too late, as belated thanks; tardy describes a person slow to arrive or act.
Procrastinate is putting off from reluctance or habit; defer is postponing by decision, often for good reason.
Deliberate means done intentionally after thought; willful adds stubborn defiance, as willful disobedience.
Premeditated is planned well in advance, usually of a crime; deliberate is intentional, whether or not planned far ahead.
Characterize is naming something's essential nature, as characterizing a speech as cautious; describe is telling what it is like in detail.
Outline is laying out the main points and how they are organized; summarize is condensing the content into a brief statement.
Revoke is canceling a right or a license granted to someone; rescind is canceling a law, an order or a decision.
Confiscate is seizing by legal authority; appropriate is taking for one's own use, often without the right to.
Withhold is refusing to give what is expected; deprive is taking away or denying what someone needs.
Abolish is formally ending a practice or an institution, as slavery; eradicate is wiping something out completely, as a disease.
Distinct means clearly separate or definite; distinctive means characteristic, marking something off from others.
Juxtapose is placing things side by side; contrast is showing how they differ, which juxtaposing may or may not do.
Divergent means moving apart from a common point, as divergent paths; disparate means fundamentally different from the start.
Dissuade is talking someone out of an action; deter is discouraging it, often through fear of consequences.
Embellish is adding decorative or exaggerated details to a true account; falsify is altering facts or records to make them false.
Skew is biasing results in one direction; distort is twisting something out of its true shape or meaning.
Diverse describes a varied group; eclectic describes a taste or method that draws from many sources.
Prevailing means currently dominant, as the prevailing view; prevalent means widespread, as a prevalent disease.
Understate is presenting something as less than it is; minimize can also mean actually reduce, as minimizing costs.
Ostensible means stated or apparent, the given reason perhaps hiding another; purported means claimed but not proven, as a purported letter.
Implausible means hard to believe; untenable means impossible to defend once challenged.
Banal is dull because unoriginal and overused; mundane is simply ordinary and everyday, not necessarily dull.
Tedious is tiresome because long or slow; monotonous is dull because unchanging.
Zealous is intensely devoted, often admired; fanatical is devoted beyond reason.
Fledgling describes a new venture or group just starting out; a novice is a person who is a beginner.
Emphasize is stressing what is true; overstate is claiming more than is true.
Dwell on is lingering, often too long, as dwelling on a mistake; focus on is directing attention, a neutral act.
Galvanize is jolting people suddenly into action; stimulate is spurring activity or growth, often gradually.
Foster is encouraging something to develop, as fostering debate; nurture adds ongoing care, as a parent nurtures a child.
An incentive is an outside reward that encourages action; a motive is the inner reason a person acts.
Menace is threatening with harm, often by presence or intent; jeopardize is putting something at risk of loss or failure.
Perennial means recurring year after year; perpetual means never stopping.
Abiding is lasting and steady, usually of a good feeling, as an abiding faith; chronic is long-lasting and recurring, usually of a problem.
Intrigued is curious and interested; rapt is completely absorbed, attention fixed.
Innate is inborn in a living being, as innate talent; inherent is built into anything, as the risks inherent in a plan.
Integral means forming an essential part of a whole; indispensable means impossible to do without.
Requisite means required; a prerequisite is required beforehand, as a course that must come first.
Legal means allowed by law; legitimate means rightful or justified, by law or by reason, as a legitimate concern.
Peruse traditionally means read carefully and thoroughly; skim means glance through quickly.
Analyze is examining the parts to see how they work; assess is judging value, quality or size after examining.
Ascertain is finding out for certain; assume is taking as true without checking.
Disseminate is spreading information widely on purpose; permeate is spreading through every part of something, as a smell permeates a room.
Explicit is stated outright; implicit is suggested but not stated.
Abet is helping along a wrongdoing; facilitate is making any task easier, usually a good one.
Facilitate is making a process easier; expedite is making it faster.
Erroneous means simply wrong, as an erroneous date; fallacious means resting on faulty reasoning, as a fallacious argument.
Counterfeit is a fake copy made to pass as the real thing, as counterfeit money; fabricated is invented outright, as fabricated evidence.
Illusory means seeming real but not; allusive means full of indirect references to other works.
Elusive means hard to catch or pin down; allusive means hinting at or referring to other works.
Vacillate is going back and forth between choices; waver is becoming unsteady or hesitant, in resolve or in motion.
Malleable means easily shaped or influenced by others; versatile means able to do many things well.
Conclude is simply ending; culminate is ending at a final high point.
Cordial is warmly polite, often formal; affable is easygoing and easy to talk to.
Amicable describes a relationship or settlement free of conflict, as an amicable parting; cordial describes warm, polite manners.
Frugal is careful with money, a virtue; parsimonious is stingy to a fault.
Futile efforts achieve nothing; counterproductive efforts make things worse.
Lavish is generous or costly in the extreme, often admiringly; extravagant stresses waste, spending beyond reason.
Nostalgic is longing specifically for the past; wistful is a vague, sad longing for anything out of reach.
Bleak means offering little hope now; ominous means warning of trouble to come.
Gradual means happening little by little; glacial means extremely slow, usually as a complaint.
Incremental is steady progress in small steps; piecemeal is bit by bit without an overall plan, often a criticism.
Insidious stresses harm that creeps in unnoticed; pernicious stresses harm that is deadly or ruinous, often hidden.
Impede is slowing progress; obstruct is blocking it, partly or wholly.
Encumber is weighing down with a burden, as encumbered by debt; hamper is getting in the way of movement or progress.
Interrupt is breaking into something briefly; disrupt is throwing its normal course into disorder.
Stymie is blocking progress so that one is stuck; thwart is defeating a plan outright.
Candid is frank by choice; ingenuous is innocently open, often from inexperience.
Veracity is truthfulness, of a person or a report; validity is logical soundness, of an argument.
Auspicious is a good sign at the start, as an auspicious beginning; propitious is conditions favorable for success, as propitious weather.
Optimistic is generally expecting good outcomes; sanguine is calmly confident even when things look bad.
Buoyant is cheerfully resilient, bouncing back; exuberant is overflowing with lively joy.
Belligerent describes a nation at war or a person openly aggressive; pugnacious describes a temperament eager to fight or argue.
Deferential is respectfully yielding to another's judgment; servile is fawningly obedient, a fault.
Modest is not boasting; self-effacing goes further, keeping oneself out of the spotlight.
Idealistic is guided by high ideals; quixotic is idealistic to the point of being foolishly impractical.
Visionary praises bold, imaginative foresight; utopian suggests an ideal too perfect to be realized.
Uninformed is lacking the facts; naive is too trusting from lack of experience.
Imply is suggesting without stating, a neutral act; insinuate is slyly hinting at something unpleasant.
Allude is referring indirectly to a person, work or event; imply is suggesting an idea without stating it.
Tacit is understood without being spoken, as tacit approval; implicit is contained in what is said without being stated outright.
Pivotal is a turning point on which the outcome depends; fundamental is basic, what everything else rests on.
Seminal describes a work that strongly influenced later work; pioneering describes being first to try something.
Paramount means of top importance; prominent means easily seen or widely known.
Rectify is correcting an error or a fault; redress is setting right a wrong done to someone, often with compensation.
Ameliorate is making a bad situation better; mitigate is making something harmful less severe.
Chronicle is recording events in the order they happened; document is recording with evidence.
Paradoxical is seemingly self-contradictory yet possibly true; contradictory is asserting two things that can't both be true.
Incongruous is strikingly out of place in its setting; inconsistent is not agreeing with itself or with other facts.
Burgeon is growing or flourishing rapidly; proliferate is multiplying rapidly in number.
Augment is adding to something to enlarge it; escalate is growing rapidly more intense or serious, as a conflict escalates.
Indifferent is not caring about a particular matter; apathetic is lacking interest or concern in general.
Blasé is unimpressed from overfamiliarity; jaded adds weariness from having had too much.
Detached is emotionally uninvolved, sometimes coldly; dispassionate is calm and fair, unswayed by emotion.
Callow is young and inexperienced, often immature; naive is too trusting, at any age.
Mediocre is only average; subpar is below the expected standard.
Strident is loud and harsh in sound or tone; vehement is forceful and passionate in feeling.
Acute is intense and sudden, as acute pain; severe is harsh or grave in degree, however it arrives.
Amplify is making something stronger or louder, a neutral act; exacerbate is making a problem worse.
Exacerbate means make a problem worse; exasperate means annoy a person intensely.
Arbitrary is based on choice or chance rather than reason; capricious is changing suddenly on a whim.
Irrelevant is unrelated to the point; extraneous is added from outside and not needed.
Magnanimous is generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival; altruistic is selflessly concerned for others' welfare.
Erudite is deeply learned, of a person; scholarly describes careful academic work or manner.
Muted is softened in color, sound or reaction, as muted applause; understated is deliberately restrained in style.
Allay is putting a fear or a doubt to rest; assuage is easing a feeling, such as grief or guilt, or satisfying a hunger.
Mollify is soothing someone's anger; placate is calming someone by giving in a little.
Alleviate is relieving pain or hardship that people feel; mitigate is reducing the severity of something harmful, as a risk or a penalty.
Measured is careful and deliberate, as a measured response; restrained is holding back feeling or force.
Ingenious is cleverly inventive in solving a problem; innovative is introducing new methods or ideas.
Radical is fundamental, going to the root of something; drastic is extreme and sudden in effect.
Neutral takes no side at all; impartial may judge between sides but favors neither.
Equal gives everyone the same; equitable gives everyone what is fair, which may differ.
Ambiguous has two or more possible meanings; vague has no clear meaning at all.
Cryptic is deliberately hard to decode, as a cryptic note; enigmatic is mysterious and hard to read, often of a person.
Redact is blacking out parts of a document so they can't be read; excise is cutting a passage or part out entirely.
Omit means leave out; emit means send out, as light, heat or gas.
Dissent is disagreeing with the majority or an official view; oppose is acting or arguing against something.
Structured is organized by a clear plan; regimented is strictly controlled, often too strictly.
Ornate is heavily decorated; opulent is lavishly rich and luxurious.
Outspoken is frank in stating opinions; vociferous is loud and insistent about them.
Overlook is missing something by accident; disregard is ignoring it on purpose.
Sketchy is lacking detail, rough; fragmentary is surviving only in broken pieces, as a fragmentary manuscript.
Passive is acted on rather than acting, by nature or by choice; inert is not moving or reacting at all, as an inert gas.
Coax is gentle, patient urging; cajole adds flattery or repeated pleading.
Cogent is convincing because clear and logical; persuasive is convincing by any means, including emotion.
Spartan stresses bare living without comforts; austere stresses severe plainness or sternness in style or manner.
Facetious is joking about something serious when joking is out of place; flippant is lightly disrespectful.
Wry is dry, mildly mocking humor; sardonic is grimly scornful mockery.
Ironic is saying the opposite of what is meant, or an outcome opposite to what was expected; sarcastic is using irony to mock or wound.
Alienate is pushing people away, as supporters; estrange is making those once close into strangers, as estranged siblings.
Pragmatic is practical and results-minded, usually approving; expedient is convenient at the cost of principle.
Feasible means possible to carry out; viable means able to succeed or survive once done.
Admire is regarding with approval; revere is deep, almost sacred respect.
Commend is praising formally, often for a specific act; laud is praising highly and publicly.
Reverent means deeply respectful; a reverend is a member of the clergy.
A harbinger is a sign announcing what is coming, as a harbinger of spring; a precursor is an earlier form that led to a later one.
A precedent is an earlier case that serves as a model; precedence is priority in order or rank.
Predict is saying what will happen; anticipate is expecting it and often preparing for it.
A person predicts; a sign or an event presages, foreshadowing what is to come.
